description:
Hi! I'm Jiya, building CLosed LOOp for the "Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge: a realistic lunar outpost game where players balance life support, radiation shielding, power and food to keep their crew alive.

The simulation engine is already built. Now we're making the dashboard and connecting NASA data.

Looking for: a UI/UX designer, a JavaScript/web developer, and someone to handle research and the demo.

If you like space and want to build something like this, join us!
summary: CLosed LOOp is a free, realistic lunar outpost game for school-age space enthusiasts, built for the “Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. Players act as mission control for four astronauts and balance power, oxygen, CO2, water, food, temperature, radiation, fatigue and crew health. Each day they set crew hours, power priorities, greenhouse lighting and shelter, then see a “You did / Result” panel linking every order to its outcome. A live Moon scene shows the shielding berm growing and the crew working. Systems are tightly linked, so one bad decision can end the mission, but players can restart and learn. Five missions include a re-run of the real August 1972 solar storm. Values come from NASA technical reports, and the game labels what is sourced, scaled or assumed. It teaches why survival off Earth depends on many systems working together.
details:
What it does and how it works. CLosed LOOp is a free, single-player, turn-based browser game. The player is mission control for a four-person lunar outpost. Each day they read the alerts and give orders: crew hours (maintenance, greenhouse, radiation shielding, cleaning panels, repairs), a power priority list for six life-support systems, greenhouse light level, and whether the crew shelters. After End day, a simulation updates power, oxygen, CO2, water, food, temperature, radiation, fatigue and crew health. A “You did / Result” panel links every order to its outcome, and a live Moon scene shows the shielding berm growing and the crew digging, cleaning, repairing or sheltering. There are five missions, from a 7-day training week to a 30-day mission with equipment failure and supply drops. One mission re-runs the real August 1972 solar particle event.

Benefits and intended impact. Students experience why survival off Earth depends on many linked systems. Dust lowers power, low power weakens the oxygen generator and CO2 scrubber, and the lunar night makes it worse. It runs on any device with nothing to install, and every control has a “?” button explaining what it does and costs.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with a separate simulation engine and a Canvas 2D Moon scene (no libraries). We used Node.js for an automated balance test, a Python build script, and GitHub Pages for hosting. Claude, an AI assistant, helped write the code.

Creativity. The game teaches through consequences, not lectures. It is strict on purpose, restarts shuffle event timing slightly, and it uses a real historic storm as a mission.

Factors we considered. Realism and honesty: every number is tagged sourced, derived, scaled or assumed, and shown in the game’s Data sources panel. Balance: eight simulated player strategies over 20 random seeds per mission. Careful play survives every mission, and careless play fails four of five. Accessibility and fairness: no install, clear explanations, and a short tour with first-time hints.
